chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Saif ibn 'Amirah from Mansur ibn Hazim from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sayyabah said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said: 'I borrow a dog belonging to a Majusi (Zoroastrian); should I hunt with it?' He said: 'Do not eat from its game, unless a Muslim taught it.'

Because the permission in the first report was directed only to the one who took the dog of the Dhimmi and taught it immediately and called it out when releasing it, and the prohibition in the second report was directed to the one who released the dog and did not teach it; therefore, it was not permissible for him to eat what it hunted. And that which indicates this is what was narrated:

key_terms.إِرْسَالِهِ: Its releasing (of the dog to hunt)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat game hunted by a dog owned by a non-Muslim?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), clarifying that the permissibility of hunting with a non-Muslim’s dog hinges on the dog being trained by a Muslim who invokes Allah’s name, thereby ensuring the ritual validity of the catch. This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the agent of consecration (*tasmiyah*) rather than mere ownership, resolving apparent contradictions in earlier reports by specifying the conditions under which the hunt is considered lawful.
